answer.rationale: The 18% spend cut and 14-day expiration window create urgency, but the assembly line running at 94% capacity means switching primary vendors (memory_c2 worked before but involved onboarding risk) or deferring is too risky given zero buffer. Adding a second source would help allocation resilience but doesn't address the cost mandate. Renewing at current terms fails the 18% target. Negotiating_terms is optimal because: (1) memory_c4 demonstrates the incumbent responds to benchmarking pressure on both price and terms; (2) memory_c6 shows multi-year commitments unlock volume pricing without narrowing scope; (3) the incumbent has proven integration stability (memory_c1), which is critical with no delivery buffer. A renegotiation can compress unit cost enough to approach the 18% target while preserving supply continuity and onboarding safety. I'm verifying memory_c4 (prior negotiation success rate and what levers moved the incumbent) and memory_c2 (to quantify what switching actually delivered, as a credible outside option for negotiation). This preserves the option to escalate to switching if negotiation fails, while treating the most likely path under time and volume constraints.
